title: A father's first advice: never set anyone beside Allah.
subtitle: What Luqman gave his son first
then: Ibn Kathir says Luqman advised the person {idea}closest and most beloved to him{/idea}, so he gave him the best he knew. He started with worshipping Allah alone. When Companions worried about a verse on wrongdoing, the Prophet ﷺ pointed them to {trap}this exact line about shirk{/trap}.
now: Your child is about to leave for university, or start a first job. You have one car ride to say what matters. Grades, money, be careful. {idea}Luqman's list started somewhere else.{/idea}
old: The most important things to teach my children are practical skills.
new: The first thing worth passing on is who to worship.
try: Tell a younger person in your family, in your own words, why you worship Allah alone.

title: She carried you in weakness upon weakness. Thank her too.
subtitle: Gratitude to Allah, then to parents
then: Ibn Kathir notes that worshipping Allah and honouring parents {idea}often come together in the Qur'an{/idea}. Here the mother is singled out: tired, stressed, up with the child night and day. The verse reminds the child of her care.
now: Your mum calls during your lunch break and you let it ring. She asks the same question twice. {reward}Once she stayed up every night with you{/reward}, and never let it ring. Allah put thanking her right next to thanking Him.
old: My parents did what parents are supposed to do.
new: What my mother carried for me deserves thanks next to my thanks to Allah.
try: Call your mother, or make dua for her if she has passed, and say thank you for one specific thing.

title: Do not obey them in shirk, but stay kind to them.
subtitle: Firm in faith, gentle with family
then: Sa'd bin Malik said this verse came about him. His mother refused to eat until he gave up Islam. {idea}He would not give it up{/idea}, and she ate. The surah introduction says young converts were told: parents have high rights, but {trap}not when they pull you to shirk{/trap}.
now: A family dinner where your choice is mocked again. You feel two pulls: give in, or walk out and stop calling. {idea}The verse holds both lines{/idea}: do not give up your faith, and keep showing up with kindness.
old: If my family opposes my faith, I either give in or walk away.
new: I can stay firm on Allah and still be gentle with them.
try: Do one kind thing for a relative you disagree with, without bringing up the disagreement.

title: A mustard seed hidden in rock, and Allah still brings it.
subtitle: Nothing small escapes Him
then: Ibn Kathir says Luqman taught his son that even a deed the size of a mustard seed {idea}will be brought out on the Day{/idea} and weighed. Allah is aware of {idea}an ant's footsteps in the darkest night{/idea}.
now: The small lie on a form. The tip you quietly left extra. The sharp comment you deleted before sending. {idea}None of it is lost.{/idea} That is a warning, and also a comfort for the good no one noticed.
old: Small things do not count. Only big deeds matter.
new: Every small deed is seen and kept, good and bad.
try: Do one tiny good deed today on purpose, knowing Allah sees it.

title: Pray, call to good, and expect to need patience.
subtitle: Luqman's advice for living it out

key.label: Why patience is in the list

then: Ibn Kathir says Luqman knew that anyone who calls to good and forbids wrong {trap}will meet harm and annoyance from people{/trap}. So he paired it with patience, calling it one of the most important commands.
now: You speak up in the office about a dodgy expense claim. Now the room is cold when you walk in. {reward}Luqman expected that.{/reward} Patience was never an extra. It was part of the plan.
old: If doing right brings trouble, maybe I did it wrong.
new: Trouble after doing right is expected, and patience is part of the deed.
try: Think of one situation where you spoke up and it cost you. Make dua for patience about it.

title: Do not turn your cheek from people or walk proudly.
subtitle: Arrogance shows in the face and the walk
then: Ibn Kathir explains: do not turn your face away when people speak to you, {trap}looking down on them{/trap}. Be gentle and {idea}greet them with a cheerful face{/idea}. Allah does not like the one who admires himself.
now: The cleaner says good morning and you nod without looking up from your phone. The junior colleague asks a question and you answer to your screen. {idea}Turn your face to them.{/idea} Small, and it changes the whole exchange.
old: I am just busy, not arrogant.
new: How I turn my face to people shows what my heart thinks of them.
try: Today, look up and smile at one person you usually rush past.

title: Walk at a moderate pace, and lower your voice.
subtitle: The closing advice of Luqman
then: Ibn Kathir says this means walking {idea}neither slow and lazy nor too fast{/idea}, and not raising your voice without need. Mujahid said a raised voice was likened to {trap}a donkey's braying{/trap} for its loudness.
now: The argument in the car park. The family debate where the loudest uncle always wins. {idea}Volume is not the same as being right.{/idea} The calmer voice is often the one people remember.
old: If I do not raise my voice, no one will take me seriously.
new: A calm, low voice carries more dignity than a loud one.
try: In your next disagreement, deliberately speak more quietly than the other person.

title: Everything is put at your service. Still some argue.
subtitle: Favours seen and unseen
then: Ibn Kathir lists the stars, rain, rivers, crops and fruits, and also {reward}the hidden favours: Messengers and Books{/reward} that remove doubts. Yet some still dispute about Allah {trap}without knowledge or proof{/trap}.
now: The phone in your hand runs on materials from the earth. The water from your tap came down as rain. {reward}The reminder that reached you today is a hidden favour too.{/reward} Arguing comes easily. Noticing takes a pause.
old: I have questions, so I can wave the whole thing away.
new: The favours around me are evidence too, if I stop to count them.
try: List five favours you used today without thinking, including one that is not physical.

title: We follow our fathers, even if the path leads to fire?
subtitle: Habit is not proof

row.title: it is what we always did

then: The surah introduction says the Makkans were invited to {idea}give up blind imitation of their forefathers{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says they had {trap}no proof except that their fathers did it{/trap}, even if Shaytan was calling them to the Fire.
now: Wedding customs, money habits, the way your family talks about other people. Some of it is good. {trap}Some of it you never questioned.{/trap} We always did it this way is a reason to look closer, not to stop looking.
old: If my family has always done it, it must be fine.
new: Habits I inherited still need checking against what Allah sent.
try: Pick one family habit and ask yourself honestly whether it pleases Allah.

title: Submit your face to Allah and hold the firmest handhold.
subtitle: Sincere surrender plus doing good
then: Ibn Kathir says submitting your face means {idea}doing deeds sincerely for His sake{/idea} and following His law. The one who does this and does good {reward}has a firm promise from Allah{/reward}.
now: The redundancy email. The test results you are waiting on. Everything you were holding feels loose. {reward}There is one handhold that does not break{/reward}: turning your whole self to Allah and doing the next good thing.
old: I feel safe when I am in control of things.
new: I am safe when I am holding on to Allah, whatever else slips.
try: When you feel anxious today, stop and say: to Allah all matters return.
